ConductAI through the ATAM lens

How should ComplaintAI and RegulatoryAI balance automation, regulatory rigor and operational speed?

Prashant Dhingra · 35-slide assessment guide

Assessment thesis

Flexible intelligence. Verifiable decisions.

This desk-based application of the Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method evaluates a shared platform with two domain engines: ComplaintAI for complaint detection and case handling, and RegulatoryAI for potential regulatory signals and applicability review.

The proposed design preserves shared evidence and domain expertise while placing authorization, effective-dated policy selection, durable approvals and tenant isolation in governed services. Detection quality must be evaluated alongside reviewer capacity, traceability and operational cost.

Assessment status: this is a concept-level pre-assessment, not a completed stakeholder workshop or empirical audit. Scenario priorities, risk ratings and architecture decisions remain provisional.

01 / Context

Business drivers and the baseline architecture

SLIDE 01

Architecture tradeoff analysis for ConductAI

This desk-based pre-assessment applies ATAM to ComplaintAI and RegulatoryAI. It moves from the supplied concept architecture to quality scenarios, tradeoffs and a refined design. It is not a completed stakeholder workshop, production audit or regulatory sign-off.

SLIDE 02

Keep intelligence flexible and control decisions

Preserve the two domain engines, strengthen the shared control plane and prove quality with evidence. AI can detect, summarize and propose; governed services authorize and persist actions, while accountable reviewers determine final findings.

SLIDE 03

Two engines on a shared trust layer

ComplaintAI detects and classifies complaints, tracks cases and recurring themes. RegulatoryAI identifies potential signals, retrieves obligations, checks applicability and routes cases for compliance review. Both depend on canonical interactions, provenance, identity, policy versions and audit records.

SLIDE 04

A synthetic cross-domain event

A customer reports an unauthorized transfer and repeated calls without an update. ComplaintAI identifies a potential complaint; RegulatoryAI identifies a potential error-resolution review. Dates, facts and applicability remain necessary, and neither engine should silently declare a violation.

SLIDE 05

Business outcomes drive the assessment

Priorities include capturing indirect complaints, surfacing relevant evidence-backed risks, reducing manual triage without flooding reviewers, and supporting multiple institutions, products, languages and policies. Model accuracy alone does not define success.

SLIDE 06

Different stakeholders see different failures

Customer service prioritizes recall and resolution; compliance needs correct obligations and evidence; audit needs replay; security needs isolation; SRE needs recovery and throughput; product needs reusable configuration. Proposed scenarios still require stakeholder voting.

SLIDE 07

The baseline architecture

Sources flow through secure ingestion, intelligence, decision control and case outcomes. Telephony, CRM, chat and email feed connectors, transcription, privacy controls and events. ComplaintAI and RegulatoryAI support workflow and review, with identity, retention, evaluation and audit across the system.

SLIDE 08

Six approaches to test

The proposed choices are a shared platform with bounded engines, hybrid AI and deterministic rules, evidence-first case records, risk-based review, event-driven processing and tenant-scoped deployment. These are design hypotheses, not assertions about implemented internals.

02 / Method

From quality goals to testable scenarios

SLIDE 09

Apply the nine ATAM steps

Present the method, business drivers and architecture; identify approaches, build a utility tree and analyze; gather and prioritize stakeholder scenarios, re-analyze and present results. The deck provides preliminary desk examples; formal stakeholder voting and evidence-based validation remain open.

SLIDE 10

Proposed quality priorities

Detection, traceability, security, human accountability and recovery receive high priority. Latency, throughput, cost and modifiability are also evaluated. Bank-specific service objectives and review requirements must replace these illustrative priorities before commitments.

SLIDE 11

The ConductAI utility tree

Correctness includes complaint recall and rule applicability; assurance includes evidence replay and approval; safety includes tenant isolation and injection defenses; operations includes surge recovery and rule changes. Use business importance and architectural difficulty for prioritization; the deck’s scenario catalogue clarifies the H/H notation.

SLIDE 12

Eight proposed scenarios

S1 tests indirect complaints; S2 effective-dated rules; S3 evidence challenged later; S4 unapproved actions; S5 cross-tenant requests; S6 adversarial email; S7 ingestion peaks; S8 policy changes. Rankings are proposals until stakeholders vote.

SLIDE 13

Specify rule applicability precisely

A compliance analyst reviews a past transaction after policy has changed. The resolver, retrieval service and case record must select the correct effective version or abstain, with evidence. Proposed measures include complete version traceability and errors on a curated test set.

03 / Deep dives

Test the boundaries that matter

SLIDE 14

S1: recall versus reviewer load

A permissive classifier may catch more indirect complaints but produce unnecessary investigations. The alternative combines calibrated thresholds, an issue taxonomy and contextual rules with exception review. Measure recall by category together with precision and review demand.

SLIDE 15

S2: a citation does not establish applicability

The proposed path filters candidate signals by product, jurisdiction, date and facts, matches approved effective-dated rule packs, checks evidence and exceptions, then routes to a reviewer. Stricter gates may reduce unsupported signals while increasing abstention and manual work.

SLIDE 16

S3: reconstruct the evidence chain

Capture source identifiers and hashes, exact transcript spans, rule provenance, model and configuration versions, reviewer decisions and replay references. Richer traceability improves reconstruction but increases privacy, retention, storage and indexing obligations.

SLIDE 17

S4: bound agent autonomy

The proposed tiers distinguish describing, detecting, recommending and deciding. Reversible internal tags differ from final findings or external filings. Service authorization must enforce the boundary; prompts alone cannot authorize restricted decisions.

SLIDE 18

S5: isolate tenants across every layer

Bind identity to a tenant, partition interactions and evidence, authorize retrieval before context construction, recheck tenant and role at every tool call, and scope audit access. Cross-tenant tests should challenge storage, retrieval, policy and tools.

SLIDE 19

S6: retrieved content is data

A malicious email may ask the agent to close a complaint and remove its risk tag. Restrict tool capabilities, validate schemas and enforce approval outside the model so document text cannot become workflow authority.

SLIDE 20

S7: buffer, route, enrich and review

Use durable events for surges, fast triage to prioritize important cases, asynchronous deep analysis with retries and checkpoints, and queues with explicit service targets. The deck’s 100,000 interactions per day is a stress-test scenario, not a verified workload.

SLIDE 21

S8: version regulatory knowledge

Propose a rule pack with source and effective dates, validate it, run golden cases and regressions, approve a signed version, then monitor. Versioned packs add governance effort but support traceability, rollback and tenant overlays better than a single prompt containing rules.

SLIDE 22

Test the full unauthorized-transfer journey

Detect the complaint, ground it in the original interaction, retrieve potential obligations, evaluate missing facts and exceptions, escalate to compliance and persist the outcome. Success means a linked complaint and reviewable signal with preserved evidence, not an unsupported legal conclusion.

04 / Findings

Compare tradeoffs and provisional risks

SLIDE 23

Compare explicit architecture alternatives

Compare general and specialist agents, prompt instructions and rule resolvers, direct writes and policy gateways, automatic finalization and human sign-off, synchronous and asynchronous analysis, and code forks versus shared cores with versioned overlays. Selection remains provisional.

SLIDE 24

Tradeoff ratings are hypotheses

Domain separation may improve ownership while adding coordination; deterministic rules support traceability but need maintenance; human sign-off adds accountability and staffing; reduced retention lowers storage exposure but weakens replay. Effects depend on workload and implementation.

SLIDE 25

Sensitivity and tradeoff points

Detection thresholds affect recall, effective dates affect correctness, tenant filters affect confidentiality and queue capacity affects disposition time. Tradeoffs arise when higher recall increases workload, richer evidence increases retention exposure or deeper analysis raises cost.

SLIDE 26

Six provisional risks

The register covers missed complaints, incorrect applicability, broken evidence chains, excessive permissions, overloaded queues and cross-bank leakage. Responses include calibration, effective-dated resolution, replay ledgers, independent gateways, capacity forecasts and isolation tests.

SLIDE 27

Conditional strengths to preserve

Separate domain engines, evidence-first records, human review and policy configuration could help meet quality goals. They become verified ATAM non-risks only after inspecting the actual implementation and test evidence.

SLIDE 28

Three business-facing risk themes

Correctness without provenance threatens defensible findings; uncontrolled delegated authority threatens action and tenant boundaries; operational overload connects detection settings to review capacity. Business, compliance, architecture, SRE and security owners should ratify priorities.

05 / Refined design

Turn findings into decisions and validation

SLIDE 29

Separate decisions from inference

The refined design combines a canonical event bus and evidence store with ComplaintAI, RegulatoryAI and a rule applicability resolver. A policy gateway and durable approvals control case actions, supported by tenant identity, privacy, audit, evaluations and observability.

SLIDE 30

Three routing outcomes

Automatically tag only low-risk reversible metadata; send ambiguous or policy-relevant signals to human review; prioritize severe harm or urgent deadlines for escalation. Confidence is considered alongside impact, applicability and permissions, not used as a substitute for authorization.

SLIDE 31

Validate each scenario

Test multilingual indirect complaints, historical rule changes, replay of 50 synthetic historical cases, unauthorized writes, cross-tenant requests, injected instructions, burst recovery and rule-pack rollback. Passing the tests reduces risk; it does not prove complete compliance or eliminate residual risk.

SLIDE 32

Record conditional architecture decisions

Preserve bounded engines; adopt effective-dated packs, an evidence ledger and a write gateway; prototype asynchronous enrichment with reviewer service targets; require scoped retrieval. Each decision needs an owner and scenario-specific acceptance evidence.

SLIDE 33

A five-week suggested sequence

Prepare architecture and permissions in week one, run stakeholder evaluation in week two, prototype boundaries in week three, test quality and operations in week four, and publish decisions and release gates in week five. Adapt this sequence to team and pilot readiness.

SLIDE 34

A provisional architecture verdict

The concept has useful shared data, domain boundaries, review and policy configuration. Key exposures remain applicability, replay, privileged tools, reviewer capacity and tenant isolation. Keep reasoning in AI, authority in governed systems and every case linked to evidence.

SLIDE 35

Sources and assessment boundaries

The deck cites CMU SEI for ATAM, NIST AI risk guidance, OWASP LLM risks and CFPB complaint-process context. It also references the earlier ConductAI enterprise design deck. This page adapts the supplied assessment; proposals remain subject to validation.

Questions, answered

ConductAI architecture assessment FAQ

What is ConductAI in this assessment?

ComplaintAI detects and classifies complaints, tracks cases and recurring themes. RegulatoryAI identifies potential signals, retrieves obligations, checks applicability and routes cases for compliance review. Both depend on canonical interactions, provenance, identity, policy versions and audit records.

Is this a completed ATAM assessment?

No. It is a desk-based pre-assessment. Formal stakeholder ranking, production testing, regulatory sign-off and a security audit have not been completed.

Why is RAG alone insufficient for rule applicability?

The proposed path filters candidate signals by product, jurisdiction, date and facts, matches approved effective-dated rule packs, checks evidence and exceptions, then routes to a reviewer. Stricter gates may reduce unsupported signals while increasing abstention and manual work.

Can RegulatoryAI automatically declare a violation?

The proposed design treats AI output as a potential signal. An authorized reviewer determines final findings; policy-controlled services enforce restricted actions.

What must be tested before approving the architecture?

Test multilingual indirect complaints, historical rule changes, replay of 50 synthetic historical cases, unauthorized writes, cross-tenant requests, injected instructions, burst recovery and rule-pack rollback. Passing the tests reduces risk; it does not prove complete compliance or eliminate residual risk.

What does H/H mean in the scenario rankings?

The scenario catalogue defines H/H as high business priority and high assessment difficulty. The utility-tree slide uses inconsistent wording; this page follows the catalogue. Rankings remain proposed until stakeholder voting.
